props.title: Asteroid

sections.content: Asteroid (1997) arrived during the late 90s disaster film boom, following the massive success of Independence Day (1996) and preceding Deep Impact (1998) and Armageddon (1998). This made-for-TV disaster film, while operating on a much smaller budget, taps into the same apocalyptic anxiety that dominated millennial sci-fi. Michael Biehn, fresh off roles in Aliens (1986) and The Abyss (1989), brings his sci-fi credibility to the role of FEMA director Jack Wallach. The film's focus on the FEMA response rather than military action sets it apart from its bigger-budget counterparts.

sections.content: The late 1990s saw a fascinating surge in asteroid-themed disaster films, reflecting both millennial anxiety and advances in CGI technology. While Asteroid took the TV movie route, its bigger-budget successors like Deep Impact (1998) and Armageddon (1998) showcased Hollywood's growing ability to visualize cosmic destruction. This trend continued into the 21st century with films like These Final Hours (2013) and Don't Look Up (2021), which used the asteroid threat as metaphors for climate change and political denial.

The scientific accuracy in asteroid disaster films varies wildly. Deep Impact (1998) consulted heavily with NASA to portray a realistic response to a cosmic threat, while Armageddon (1998) famously took creative liberties that NASA now uses in their training program as examples of what not to do. Asteroid, despite its limitations, actually presents some plausible scenarios in terms of emergency response protocols. SUBHEAD: Evolution of Cosmic Disaster Films

movies.title: Don't Look Up
movies.slug: Two astronomers try to warn humanity about an approaching comet while facing political and media indifference.

sections.content: The cosmic disaster genre has evolved significantly since When Worlds Collide (1951), which pioneered many tropes still used today. Meteor (1979) starring Sean Connery marked the first major modern asteroid disaster film, followed by the TV movie Without Warning (1994). By the time Asteroid aired, the genre had established clear patterns: discovery, denial, preparation, and last-minute heroics. Recent entries like Greenland (2020) focus more on personal survival stories than grand-scale prevention efforts.
